nameStory: This lilac honors Baroness Julia Jósika, a 19th-century Hungarian noblewoman who was passionate about botany and horticulture. The species was named Syringa josikaea in her honor, making her one of the few women to have a lilac species bear her name.
description: Hungarian lilac is a large, sturdy shrub that can grow 8-12 feet tall and wide, creating an impressive presence in the landscape. Unlike the familiar common lilac, this species has a more upright, vase-like growth habit with thick, sturdy branches. It produces fragrant purple flower clusters in late spring to early summer, though they're typically smaller and less showy than those of common lilac. The leaves are notably thick and leathery, giving the entire plant a robust, almost wild appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery leaves that feel almost rubbery to the touch, with a glossy dark green upper surface and paler underside. They're arranged in opposite pairs and have a distinctive oval shape with pointed tips.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, upright clusters of small purple flowers that smell sweetly fragrant, blooming later than common lilac (typically June). Each tiny flower has four petals and the clusters are more compact and narrow than other lilacs.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a large, upright shrub with a vase-like shape and thick, sturdy stems that feel quite rigid when bent. The overall appearance is more robust and wild-looking than the refined common lilac.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray-brown bark on younger stems that becomes slightly furrowed with age. The stems are notably thick and feel very solid compared to other lilac species.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Large, plump winter buds that are reddish-brown and arranged opposite each other along the stems. They're noticeably bigger and more robust than common lilac buds.

habitat: In New England, Hungarian lilac is primarily found in cultivated settings like botanical gardens, arboretums, and specialty landscaping projects rather than naturalized in the wild. When planted, it thrives in well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade, often used in areas where a hardy, late-blooming lilac is desired. It's much more tolerant of difficult growing conditions than common lilac.

seasonality.spring: Thick, leathery leaves emerge later than common lilac, typically in late April to May. The robust leaf texture becomes apparent immediately as new growth unfolds.
seasonality.summer: Purple flower clusters bloom in June, later than most other lilacs, filling the air with sweet fragrance. The thick, glossy leaves remain dark green and substantial throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, though fall color is usually not spectacular. The sturdy branch structure becomes more visible as leaves begin to thin.
seasonality.winter: Large, plump reddish-brown buds are prominent along the thick, gray-brown stems. The robust branching pattern and substantial stem thickness help distinguish it from other lilacs even when bare.

funFact: Hungarian lilac is actually a living fossil - paleobotanists have found evidence that this species once grew across much of central Europe during prehistoric times, but now survives naturally in only a tiny area of the Carpathian Mountains, making every cultivated plant a conservation ambassador for this ancient lineage.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with common lilac, but Hungarian lilac's thick, leathery leaves feel distinctly different - almost rubbery compared to common lilac's thinner, softer foliage. Memory trick: 'Hungarian = Hardy' - everything about this plant feels more substantial and tough.
contextualKnowledge: With only 4 recorded observations in New England, Hungarian lilac is quite rare in our region and is primarily found in specialized collections rather than typical home landscapes. Many people assume all lilacs are the same species, but Hungarian lilac represents just one of several distinct lilac species, each with unique characteristics.
compareHints: Hungarian lilac differs from common lilac in its much thicker, leathery leaves, later bloom time, and more upright growth habit. Compared to Japanese tree lilac, it stays shrub-sized rather than becoming tree-like, and its flowers are purple rather than creamy white. Korean lilac is much smaller overall, while Hungarian lilac is notably robust and substantial in all its parts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common lilac blooms earlier than Japanese tree lilac and has the classic sweet fragrance, while tree lilac has a honey-like scent and blooms in June.
Japanese tree lilac is easily distinguished from common lilac and other shrubby lilacs by its tree form and creamy-white, honey-scented flowers that bloom much later in the season.
Korean lilac is much more compact than common lilac, staying under 6 feet versus 15+ feet, and has smaller, fuzzier leaves.
